cards.title: Simultaneous polynomial-length constant-space refutations
cards.formal: Is the following statement true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\) and every family \((F_n)_{n\ge1}\) of unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF formulas of size polynomial in \(n\), if there is a constant \(s\) such that every \(F_n\) has a resolution refutation using at most \(s\) clauses simultaneously, then there are constants \(S\ge1\), \(C>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that every \(F_n\) has a single resolution refutation \(\pi_n\) with \[\operatorname{Sp}(\pi_n)\le S\qquad\text{and}\qquad L(\pi_n)\le C(n+1)^d.\] The constants may depend on the family and on \(k,s\), but not on \(n\). In particular, the conclusion may use a larger constant space bound \(S\) than the original bound \(s\).
cards.why: Proof length measures how many lines a refutation generates, and clause space measures how many it must retain at once. The question asks whether a formula that is easy in each measure separately can be hard when both restrictions apply to the same proof. Its constant-space regime makes it a sharp structural question about resolution and the interpretation of proof-memory bounds.
cards.status_note: The question is explicit in the 2013 survey and is revisited as unresolved in the checked 2022 primary paper. Its 2023 journal abstract reports a restricted polynomial lower bound rather than a resolution. Bounded later-work checks through 2026-09-15 found no proof or refutation of the full constant-space statement. This review does not independently certify every subsequent proof or an exhaustive literature search.

importance.reason: A basic unresolved compatibility question between two central resolution resources. Constant clause space already implies the existence of polynomial-length proofs separately, while known severe trade-offs at growing space do not determine whether the two bounds can always coexist at constant space.

sentences: The question asks whether every fixed-width CNF family with constant-clause-space refutations also has refutations that are both polynomial-length and constant-clause-space.
The same proof must meet both bounds, but its allowed constant space may exceed the original one.
Space counts stored clauses regardless of their lengths, while proof length counts downloads and inferences.
Known separate short-proof guarantees and results for constant total literal space do not provide the requested simultaneous clause-space bound.
The later checked work still poses the question and proves only a polynomial lower bound for a restricted tree-like setting.

cards.definitions: Variables are drawn from a countable set. A literal is a variable or its negation. A clause is a finite set of literals, interpreted as their disjunction, and a CNF formula is a finite set of clauses, interpreted as their conjunction. A \(k\)-CNF has at most \(k\) literals per input clause; derived clauses have no width bound. Define the size of \(F\) to be \(\sum_{A\in F}(1+|A|)\). Polynomial size means that some \(a>0,b\in\mathbb N\), fixed for the family, satisfy this size bound \(\le a(n+1)^b\) for every \(n\). The parameter \(n\) indexes the family; it need not equal the number of variables. There is no computability or uniform generation requirement on the family. A proof is a finite sequence of configurations \(\mathcal C_0,\ldots,\mathcal C_t\), each a finite set of clauses, starting at \(\mathcal C_0=\varnothing\). One step may add an input clause from \(F\); add the resolvent \(A\cup B\) when \(A\cup\{x\}\) and \(B\cup\{\neg x\}\) are both currently present, with \(x\) absent from \(A\) and \(\neg x\) absent from \(B\); add a weakening \(A\cup B\) when \(A\) is present and \(B\) is any finite clause; or erase one currently present clause. An inference adds its conclusion before any separate erasure, so premises and conclusion coexist in that configuration. The proof ends with the empty clause present. The clause space is \(\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)=\max_j|\mathcal C_j|\), counting input clauses only while they have been downloaded and retained. The length \(L(\pi)\) is the number of input-clause downloads and inference steps, including weakenings and rederivations, but excluding erasures. Erased clauses may be downloaded or derived again; their reappearance is charged again. There is no read-once, tree-like, regularity or restriction on reuse. Space counts clauses regardless of how many literals they contain: it is not total literal space, variable space, bit memory or width. Length counts proof lines as specified, not the bit cost of manipulating a long clause. The target concerns existence of proofs with the two simultaneous bounds, not an efficient algorithm that finds them.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated implication for every fixed width and every polynomial-size family, or prove its negation. A positive answer must produce or establish existence of refutations satisfying both resource bounds at once. Separate witnesses for polynomial length and constant clause space do not suffice. A negative answer must exhibit a fixed \(k\) and a polynomial-size family with a common constant-space refutation bound, but such that for every \(S\ge1,C>0,d\in\mathbb N\) some member has no refutation satisfying both \(\operatorname{Sp}(\pi)\le S\) and \(L(\pi)\le C(n+1)^d\). A polynomial length lower bound, a lower bound only for tree-like proofs, or a trade-off that disappears after increasing space by a fixed constant does not refute this statement.

context_blocks.text: Nordström’s Open Problem 16 asks this simultaneous length–clause-space question for polynomial-size fixed-width CNF families. It is distinct from the neighboring question about trade-offs when space is at least linear in formula size, whose later resolution is already noted in the survey.

The survey records that a constant clause-space bound guarantees some polynomial-length refutation, but that conclusion does not bound the clause space of the short refutation. The missing simultaneous guarantee is precisely the present target.

With total literal space in place of clause space, the corresponding simultaneous constant-space and polynomial-length statement is already known. A constant number of clauses may nevertheless contain many literals, so that result does not apply to this measure.

Papamakarios and Razborov’s ICALP 2022 paper revisits the same constant-clause-space question explicitly in Section 5. Theorem 4.7 gives formulas of linear size with clause-space-four tree-like refutations for which all tree-like refutations have a nearly quadratic length lower bound. A polynomial lower bound in that restricted proof system does not contradict the present unrestricted polynomial-length conclusion.

Their broader equivalences relate proof-space measures to tree-like proof size and identify stronger separation questions. The checked journal metadata places the expanded publication in November 2023; the theorem numbering quoted here is from the fully read ICALP version.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
